extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, in-house counsel, and judges handling patent infringement litigation
extracted.subtask_description: Standards for pleading patent eligibility under 35 U.S.C. § 101 (Alice framework) and for pleading willful/indirect infringement at the Rule 12(b)(6) stage in patent litigation. Includes when claims may be treated as representative and guidance on amendment for post-filing knowledge allegations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 8 / Rule 12(b)(6) pleading standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 8 requires a complainant to provide 'a short and plain statement of the claim showing that the pleader is entitled to relief.' Rule 12(b)(6) allows dismissal if the complaint fails to meet that standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 12(b)(6) motion may be granted only if, accepting the well-pleaded allegations in the complaint as true and viewing them in the light most favorable to the complainant, a court concludes those allegations 'could not raise a claim of entitlement to relief.' (Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative-claim treatment at pleading stage
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim may be treated as 'representative' for purposes of a § 101 eligibility analysis when briefing does not present any meaningful argument for the distinctive significance of any claim limitations other than those in the representative claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use representative-claim treatment where the plaintiff's briefing refers generally to the 'Asserted Patents' and does not make arguments relying on limitations found only in other claims (Elec. Power Grp. v. Alstom).

rubrics_metrics.name: §101 / Alice two-step framework
rubrics_metrics.description: First determine whether the claims are drawn to a patent-ineligible concept (laws of nature, natural phenomena, abstract ideas). If yes, then look to the elements of the claim individually and as an ordered combination to determine whether there is an 'inventive concept' sufficient to ensure the patent amounts to 'significantly more' than the ineligible concept itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim that recites an abstract idea must include additional features that ensure it is more than a drafting effort to monopolize the idea. The mere recitation of a generic computer cannot transform an abstract idea into patent-eligible subject matter (Alice; Mayo).

rubrics_metrics.name: When §101 can be decided on the pleadings
rubrics_metrics.description: §101 is a threshold legal issue and may be raised at the pleading stage if it is apparent from the face of the patent that the asserted claims are not directed to eligible subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is appropriate only when there are no factual allegations that, taken as true, prevent resolving eligibility as a matter of law (Cleveland Clinic; Aatrix Software). If factual disputes exist, §101 should not be resolved on a motion to dismiss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate claims in light of specification and identified technical problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should be considered as a whole in light of the specification; where the specification identifies a specific problem in the prior art and the claims recite a specific solution (an improvement to computer functionality), the claims may be patent-eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precedent recognizes that specific technological modifications to solve a problem or improve the functioning of a known system generally produce patent-eligible subject matter (Core Wireless, Trading Techs, Data Engine). Look for specification language describing prior-art problems and specific structural/functional improvements (e.g., interactive links/reference indicators improving messaging GUI).

rubrics_metrics.name: Real-world analogy not dispositive
rubrics_metrics.description: Tracing the invention to some real-world analogy (e.g., characteristics of human conversation) is not, by itself, sufficient to render a claim abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the claimed concept has an analog in human behavior, the court must assess whether the claim as a whole provides a concrete technological solution or merely recites an abstract idea implemented on generic technology (Data Engine).

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional/results-only claim language signals ineligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that contain only results-based and functional language and lack any explanation of how to achieve the desired result are hallmarks of ineligible claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare such claims to those that recite a specific structure performing a function (e.g., 'notebook tabs' or specific GUI elements); reciting a specific structure within a particular display that performs a specific function can support eligibility (Data Engine).

rubrics_metrics.name: Willful infringement substantive standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Willfulness requires a finding of 'deliberate or intentional' infringement; subjective willfulness can be satisfied by proof that the defendant acted in the face of a risk of infringement that was 'either known or so obvious that it should have been known' to the accused infringer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Halo and WesternGeco standards: willfulness focuses on the defendant's bad state of mind and requires evidence beyond mere infringement and knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-suit knowledge requirement for induced and willful infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegations of pre-suit knowledge are necessary to support claims of willful and induced infringement based on pre-suit conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific factual allegations (e.g., an inventor emailed a company VP with a link to a presentation that included the patent number and the VP acknowledged receipt) can plausibly allege pre-suit knowledge. General allegations (e.g., defendant is a 'sophisticated corporate entity' or that prosecution was 'public record') are insufficient without more specific facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of post-suit knowledge and amendment rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A complaint generally does not operate going forward to establish knowledge for post-suit willfulness/inducement; plaintiffs should be allowed to amend to allege knowledge acquired since filing for indirect infringement but post-suit willfulness allegations are usually implausible alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For indirect infringement, courts may permit amendment to allege knowledge since filing because otherwise indirect infringement claims could be foreclosed. For willfulness, post-suit allegations typically fail absent pre-suit knowledge or other specific facts showing a culpable mind; evidence of post-suit bad conduct is often privileged (advice of counsel), making such allegations difficult to plead plausibly. The court here granted leave to amend limitedly (two weeks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausibility requirement for knowledge/bad-mind allegations
rubrics_metrics.description: A plaintiff must plead sufficient factual matter to make allegations of knowledge or willfulness plausible, not merely conceivable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bare assertions or reliance on public-knowledge statements are inadequate. The complaint must contain factual details that, if true, plausibly support the inference of knowledge or culpable intent (Mayer v. Belichick; district-level examples cited).
